conflicts/german-peasants-war/religionRo: The grievances behind the war — serfdom, rising dues and tithes, loss of common woods, waters and pastures, and lords' encroachment on village self-government — were old, and earlier risings such as the Bundschuh and Poor Conrad (1514) had no Protestant element. What was new in 1525 was the language of the Reformation: the ‘pure gospel’ and ‘divine law’ (göttliches Recht), which turned local complaints into a programme for a Christian social order. Peter Blickle called it a ‘revolution of the common man’ legitimised by the gospel; Marxist historians, following Engels, saw an early bourgeois revolution with Thomas Müntzer as its hero; Tom Scott and Bob Scribner stress regional variety and economic causes. Most historians now agree that religion did not cause the war but decisively shaped its ideology and scale, while Müntzer's apocalyptic theology made the Thuringian rising an explicitly holy war.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/sides/0/fa: Evangelical and radical Reformation sympathies, many still Catholic in practice
conflicts/german-peasants-war/summary: In 1524–25 the largest popular uprising in Europe before the French Revolution swept through southern and central Germany. Hundreds of thousands of peasants and townspeople, inspired by Reformation preaching, demanded the abolition of serfdom and a social order based on ‘divine law’. The princes, Catholic and Lutheran together, crushed the rising in a few weeks of battles and reprisals that killed tens of thousands, while Luther's call to ‘smite, slay and stab’ the rebels permanently shaped the Reformation's relationship to the state.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/story:
Southern Germany in the early sixteenth century was a patchwork of lordships in which peasants faced growing burdens: lords revived or extended serfdom, raised dues and death-duties, restricted access to woods, rivers and common pasture, and tightened their courts. Secret peasant leagues under the sign of the laced peasant boot, the Bundschuh, had plotted risings in 1493, 1502, 1513 and 1517, and the Poor Conrad rebellion shook Württemberg in 1514. From 1520 the preaching of Luther and others gave these grievances a new vocabulary. Luther's Freedom of a Christian, the attack on clerical wealth and tithes, and the demand that congregations be fed the ‘pure gospel’ suggested that existing burdens had no basis in Scripture.

The war began in the summer of 1524 in the landgraviate of Stühlingen, near the Swiss border — according to a later story when the countess demanded that her peasants collect snail shells for winding yarn during harvest. Through the winter, unrest spread across the Black Forest, the Hegau and Upper Swabia. In February and March 1525 large armed assemblies formed at Baltringen, around Lake Constance and in the Allgäu, and on 7 March their delegates met at Memmingen and formed the Christian Union of Upper Swabia. There the furrier and lay preacher Sebastian Lotzer, probably with the town's preacher Christoph Schappeler, drafted the Twelve Articles. They asked for congregations to choose their own pastors, for the abolition of the ‘small tithe’ and of serfdom — ‘since Christ has redeemed us all with his precious blood’ — for free hunting, fishing and wood-gathering, and for fair rents and justice, and promised to withdraw any article shown to be contrary to Scripture. Printed in some 25 editions within two months, they became the manifesto of the whole movement.

In April and May the rising spread to Franconia, Württemberg, Alsace, Thuringia, Saxony, Tyrol and Salzburg. Peasant bands stormed and burned castles and monasteries, often plundering their wine cellars, and forced nobles and towns to join their ‘Christian brotherhood’. On Easter Sunday, 16 April 1525, the Odenwald band took Weinsberg and made Count Ludwig von Helfenstein and other nobles run a gauntlet of pikes before the eyes of his wife — an atrocity that hardened opinion against the peasants everywhere. In Thuringia Thomas Müntzer, the radical preacher of Mühlhausen, declared that the time of the harvest had come, that the godless had no right to live and that the sword had been given to the elect; he signed his letters ‘Thomas Müntzer with the sword of Gideon’.

Luther at first, in his Admonition to Peace (April 1525), rebuked the lords for their tyranny as well as the peasants for using the gospel to justify rebellion. After touring Thuringia and hearing of Weinsberg he wrote Against the Robbing and Murdering Hordes of Peasants, urging the princes to ‘smite, slay and stab, secretly or openly’, for nothing could be more poisonous than a rebel. It appeared as the princes were already striking back. The Swabian League's army under Georg Truchsess von Waldburg — the ‘Bauernjörg’ — had defeated a peasant force at Leipheim on 4 April and negotiated the Treaty of Weingarten with the Lake Constance band on 17 April; on 12 May it routed the Württemberg peasants at Böblingen and burned Weinsberg in reprisal.

The decisive blow fell in Thuringia. On 15 May 1525 the armies of Philip of Hesse, Duke George of Saxony and Duke Henry of Brunswick attacked about 8,000 poorly armed peasants in their wagon fort above Frankenhausen while negotiations were still going on. Müntzer had promised that he would catch the cannonballs in his sleeve; a rainbow, his emblem, is said to have appeared over the field. Some 5,000–6,000 peasants were killed for a handful of princely losses. Müntzer was found hiding in the town, tortured, and beheaded with Heinrich Pfeiffer outside Mühlhausen on 27 May. Two days after Frankenhausen, Duke Antoine of Lorraine's army massacred thousands of Alsatian peasants at Saverne after they had surrendered. In Franconia the Swabian League destroyed the peasant armies at Königshofen on 2 June and Ingolstadt on 4 June, where Florian Geyer's Black Band was annihilated, and relieved the besieged fortress of Würzburg.

Reprisals followed: executions, mutilations, villages burned, and heavy fines that took years to pay. Pockets of resistance continued in Salzburg and Tyrol, where Michael Gaismair drew up a radical Tyrolean constitution (1526) for an egalitarian Christian commonwealth before he fled to Venice. The Diet of Speyer in 1526 recommended some moderation in lords' demands, and in parts of the south-west peasants gained limited rights through negotiated settlements and courts.

The defeat had lasting consequences for the Reformation. Luther's movement, already distrustful of popular radicalism, bound itself to the princes, who became the guardians of the territorial churches. Catholic polemicists blamed Luther for the bloodshed, while the bloody end of Müntzer's apocalyptic crusade helped push the emerging Anabaptists in Switzerland and South Germany towards the renunciation of the sword at Schleitheim in 1527. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the war became a contested national memory: Engels and East German historians celebrated Müntzer as a revolutionary, the GDR built a vast panorama painting at Bad Frankenhausen, and church historians continued to debate Luther's role.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/nameOfGod: The rebels claimed to stand for ‘the gospel and divine justice’: the Twelve Articles grounded every demand in Scripture, arguing that serfdom was incompatible with Christ's redemption of all, and called their alliance the ‘Christian Union’ or ‘Christian brotherhood’. Peasant banners bore the cross, the crucifix and the rainbow. Müntzer preached to the princes on Daniel 2 (July 1524) that the sword was given to rulers to destroy the godless and would pass to the people if they failed, told the miners of Mansfeld ‘at them, at them, while the fire is hot’, and promised the Frankenhausen army divine protection. On the other side Luther invoked Romans 13 to declare that rebels forfeit their lives before God and that a prince killing a rebel could ‘win heaven with bloodshed’.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/religiousC: Evangelical preaching of the ‘pure gospel’ and the priesthood of all believers encouraged villagers to judge their lords' demands by Scripture and to demand the right to choose their own pastors.
The concept of ‘divine law’ (göttliches Recht), drawn from Reformation preaching, replaced appeals to ‘old law’ and custom with a universal Christian standard against serfdom and unjust dues.
Anticlericalism and resentment of ecclesiastical lords — abbeys and prince-bishoprics were among the harshest landlords — made monasteries prime targets.
Thomas Müntzer's apocalyptic theology, which taught that the elect must take the sword against the godless before Christ's return, turned the Thuringian rising into a holy war.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/otherCause: Lords were reimposing and extending serfdom, death duties and labour services in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries.
Population growth, rising prices and pressure on land made the enclosure of commons, forests and fishing rights especially bitter.
Territorial princes were consolidating their states, undermining the autonomy of village communities and their courts.
A tradition of peasant conspiracies (the Bundschuh) and the example of the Swiss, who had freed themselves from lords, encouraged armed resistance.
In the towns, journeymen and poorer citizens joined the rising against urban oligarchies.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/triggers/0: The Stühlingen peasants' refusal of labour services in June 1524, which began a chain of local strikes and assemblies.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/triggers/1: The formation of the Christian Union of Upper Swabia at Memmingen in March 1525 and the rapid printing of the Twelve Articles.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/triggers/2: The absence of the Swabian League's troops in Italy during the war with France, which left lords without force in early 1525.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/0: June: the Stühlingen peasants rise; in July Müntzer preaches his Sermon to the Princes at Allstedt.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/1: September: Conrad Grebel and his Zurich circle write to Müntzer urging him not to defend the gospel with the sword.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/2: February–March: armed bands assemble at Baltringen, Lake Constance and the Allgäu; the Christian Union forms at Memmingen and the Twelve Articles are printed.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/3: 4 April: the Swabian League defeats peasants at Leipheim; 16 April: the Weinsberg massacre of nobles.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/4: 17 April: Treaty of Weingarten; Luther publishes his Admonition to Peace.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/5: May: Luther's Against the Robbing and Murdering Hordes of Peasants; 12 May: peasants routed at Böblingen.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/6: 15 May: massacre at Frankenhausen; 17 May: slaughter of Alsatian peasants at Saverne; 27 May: Müntzer beheaded at Mühlhausen.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/7: 2–4 June: Franconian peasants destroyed at Königshofen and Ingolstadt; Würzburg relieved.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/8: Michael Gaismair's Tyrolean constitution; the Salzburg rising is suppressed; the Diet of Speyer urges moderation.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/timeline/9: The Schleitheim Confession of the Swiss Brethren renounces the sword for Christians.

conflicts/german-peasants-war/casualties: The figure of about 100,000 dead, repeated since the sixteenth century, is traditional and probably an upper estimate; many modern historians prefer ‘70,000–100,000’ or simply ‘tens of thousands’. Most victims were peasants killed in a few one-sided battles and their aftermath (perhaps 5,000–6,000 at Frankenhausen and several thousand at Saverne) and in subsequent executions; noble and princely losses were very small. No systematic count was made.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/effects/0: The rising was crushed everywhere except in a few areas where negotiated settlements brought modest relief; serfdom persisted in much of Germany for centuries.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/effects/1: Princely power grew, and the German peasantry did not rise on such a scale again before the nineteenth century.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/effects/2: Some territories, through courts and treaties such as those in Kempten and Tyrol, offered limited legal redress for peasant grievances.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/effects/3: The war became a powerful symbol in later German politics, claimed by liberals, nationalists and especially by Marxists and the German Democratic Republic.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/effectsOnC: Luther's movement bound itself to the territorial princes, who directed the Lutheran churches through church ordinances and visitations from 1526–27.
Catholic opponents blamed the Reformation for the rising, and the experience pushed several territories and cities back towards Rome.

The emerging Anabaptist movement, partly associated with the rebels in Waldshut and Thuringia, turned decisively to non-resistance at Schleitheim in 1527, while authorities treated all Anabaptists as potential revolutionaries.
The failure of Müntzer's crusade discredited apocalyptic violence for most Protestants, though Melchiorite apocalypticism would return at Münster.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/legacy: The Peasants' War marked the point at which the Reformation ceased to be a popular movement of the ‘common man’ and became a reform managed by princes and city councils. Luther's harsh pamphlet remains one of the most debated texts of his career, and the Lutheran World Federation and German churches marked the 500th anniversary in 2025 with reflection on his role. Müntzer's memory has passed from heretic to revolutionary icon to a subject of nuanced theological study.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/dissenters: In a letter of September 1524 the Zurich radicals told Müntzer that the gospel and its followers ‘are not to be protected by the sword, nor are they thus to protect themselves’, and urged him to give up preaching violence against the godless.
The Lutheran reformer of Schwäbisch Hall wrote in 1525 urging princes to show mercy to defeated peasants and condemning indiscriminate reprisals.

Before turning against the rebels, Luther told the lords that God was punishing their tyranny and urged both sides to arbitration rather than war, while denying that the gospel could justify rebellion.

A former Benedictine prior whose abbey was occupied by peasants, he became an Anabaptist and in the Schleitheim Confession (1527) declared the sword ‘outside the perfection of Christ’; he was executed at Rottenburg in 1527.
conflicts/german-peasants-war/campaigns/: Georg Truchsess von Waldburg and the army of the Swabian League

From Ulm the League's army crushed the Baltringen band at Leipheim, made terms with the Lake Constance peasants at Weingarten, routed the Württembergers at Böblingen, burned Weinsberg in revenge, and destroyed the Franconian armies at Königshofen before entering Würzburg in June.
Philip of Hesse, Duke George of Saxony and Duke Henry of Brunswick

Philip of Hesse subdued the Fulda peasants in early May, marched through Thuringia, joined the Saxon and Brunswick forces before Frankenhausen on 15 May, then received the surrender of Mühlhausen, where Müntzer and Pfeiffer were executed.

Expelled from Allstedt after his Sermon to the Princes, Müntzer went to Mühlhausen, printed tracts in Nuremberg and spent the winter among the rebellious peasants of the Klettgau and Hegau before returning to Mühlhausen and leading its men to Frankenhausen.
